items.title: 10.7 Express the Product (of sines and cosines) as Sums or Differences (of sines and cosines)

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: In 10.3 we expanded \(\sin(\alpha \pm \beta)\) and \(\cos(\alpha \pm \beta)\) into products like \(\sin\alpha\cos\beta\). This section goes the other way round: it turns a product of sines and cosines into a sum or difference, and then a sum or difference into a product. The trick is simple: add or subtract two of the known formulas so that one term cancels.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: Identity (vii) is printed as \(\cos(\alpha + \beta) - \cos(\alpha - \beta) = 2\cos\alpha\cos\beta\). Adding (iii) and (iv) gives a plus sign: \(\cos(\alpha + \beta) + \cos(\alpha - \beta) = 2\cos\alpha\cos\beta\) (the \(\sin\alpha\sin\beta\) terms cancel). The book's own box below uses the correct \(+\).

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: Why do these work? In (i) and (ii) the terms \(\cos\alpha\sin\beta\) have opposite signs, so adding cancels them and subtracting doubles them. In (iii) and (iv) the terms \(\sin\alpha\sin\beta\) have opposite signs, so adding cancels them and subtracting doubles them. Be careful with (viii): subtracting gives \(-\sin\alpha\sin\beta - \sin\alpha\sin\beta = -2\sin\alpha\sin\beta\).
So, we get four identities as:

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
How to choose: look at the product.
\(\sin \times \cos\) (sine first): use the first line.
\(\cos \times \sin\) (cosine first): use the second line.
\(\cos \times \cos\): use the third line.
\(\sin \times \sin\): use the fourth line, and do not forget its minus sign.
Write the larger angle as \(\alpha\) so that \(\alpha - \beta\) is positive. Each formula needs the factor 2 in front; if it is missing, multiply and divide by 2.

Now putting \(\alpha + \beta = P\) and \(\alpha - \beta = Q\), we get
\[\alpha + \beta = P, \quad \alpha - \beta = Q\]
\[\alpha = \dfrac{P + Q}{2}, \quad \beta = \dfrac{P - Q}{2}\]

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: The step the book leaves out: add the two equations, \(2\alpha = P + Q\), so \(\alpha = \frac{P + Q}{2}\); subtract them, \(2\beta = P - Q\), so \(\beta = \frac{P - Q}{2}\). Putting these into the four product identities gives the next box. In words: half the sum and half the difference of the two angles.

blocks.title: Sum and difference identities
blocks.text:
\[\sin P + \sin Q\]
\[= 2\sin\dfrac{P + Q}{2}\cos\dfrac{P - Q}{2}\]
\[\sin P - \sin Q\]
\[= 2\cos\dfrac{P + Q}{2}\sin\dfrac{P - Q}{2}\]
\[\cos P + \cos Q\]
\[= 2\cos\dfrac{P + Q}{2}\cos\dfrac{P - Q}{2}\]
\[\cos P - \cos Q\]
\[= -2\sin\dfrac{P + Q}{2}\sin\dfrac{P - Q}{2}\]

blocks.title: Exam tip
blocks.text:
A short way to remember the box:
sin + sin = 2 sin(half sum) cos(half difference)
sin − sin = 2 cos(half sum) sin(half difference)
cos + cos = 2 cos(half sum) cos(half difference)
cos − cos = −2 sin(half sum) sin(half difference)
Only the last one has a minus sign, and in every line the half sum comes first.

blocks.title: Example 14
blocks.problem: Express \(2\sin 7\theta\cos 3\theta\) as a sum or difference.
steps:
Given: the product \(2\sin 7\theta\cos 3\theta\).
To find: the same expression as a sum or difference.
Method: it is \(2\sin\alpha\cos\beta\) (sine first, then cosine), so use \(2\sin\alpha\cos\beta = \sin(\alpha + \beta) + \sin(\alpha - \beta)\).

Step 1: Identify the angles
\[\alpha = 7\theta, \quad \beta = 3\theta\]
Why: matching the expression with the left side of the formula tells us what to put in the right side.

Step 2: Apply the formula
\[2\sin 7\theta\cos 3\theta\]
\[= \sin(7\theta + 3\theta) + \sin(7\theta - 3\theta)\]
\[= \sin 10\theta + \sin 4\theta\]
Why: \(7\theta + 3\theta = 10\theta\) and \(7\theta - 3\theta = 4\theta\).

Check: take \(\theta = 15^{\circ}\), so \(7\theta = 105^{\circ}\), \(3\theta = 45^{\circ}\).
\[2\sin 105^{\circ}\cos 45^{\circ}\]
\[= 2\cdot\dfrac{\sqrt{6} + \sqrt{2}}{4}\cdot\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2} = \dfrac{\sqrt{3} + 1}{2}\]
\[\sin 150^{\circ} + \sin 60^{\circ} = \dfrac{1}{2} + \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\]
Both sides equal \(\frac{1 + \sqrt{3}}{2}\).

blocks.title: Example 15
blocks.problem: Prove without using table / calculator, that \(\sin 19^{\circ}\cos 11^{\circ} + \sin 71^{\circ}\sin 11^{\circ} = \frac{1}{2}\)
steps:
Given: \(\sin 19^{\circ}\cos 11^{\circ} + \sin 71^{\circ}\sin 11^{\circ}\).
To prove: it equals \(\frac{1}{2}\) without tables.
Method: \(19^{\circ}\), \(11^{\circ}\), \(71^{\circ}\) are not standard angles, but their sums and differences (\(30^{\circ}\), \(60^{\circ}\), \(82^{\circ}\), \(8^{\circ}\)) are useful. So change both products into sums with the product identities.

Step 1: Create the factor 2
\[\text{L.H.S.} = \sin 19^{\circ}\cos 11^{\circ} + \sin 71^{\circ}\sin 11^{\circ}\]
\[= \dfrac{1}{2}\left[2\sin 19^{\circ}\cos 11^{\circ}\right.\]
\[\left.\quad + 2\sin 71^{\circ}\sin 11^{\circ}\right]\]
Why: the product identities have \(2\sin\alpha\cos\beta\) and \(2\sin\alpha\sin\beta\); multiplying by 2 and dividing by 2 keeps the value the same.

Step 2: First product
\[2\sin 19^{\circ}\cos 11^{\circ}\]
\[= \sin(19^{\circ} + 11^{\circ}) + \sin(19^{\circ} - 11^{\circ})\]
\[= \sin 30^{\circ} + \sin 8^{\circ}\]
Why: \(2\sin\alpha\cos\beta = \sin(\alpha + \beta) + \sin(\alpha - \beta)\) with \(\alpha = 19^{\circ}\), \(\beta = 11^{\circ}\).

Step 3: Second product
\[2\sin 71^{\circ}\sin 11^{\circ}\]
\[= -\left[\cos(71^{\circ} + 11^{\circ}) - \cos(71^{\circ} - 11^{\circ})\right]\]
\[= -\cos 82^{\circ} + \cos 60^{\circ}\]
Why: from \(-2\sin\alpha\sin\beta = \cos(\alpha + \beta) - \cos(\alpha - \beta)\) we get \(2\sin\alpha\sin\beta = -[\cos(\alpha + \beta) - \cos(\alpha - \beta)]\), with \(\alpha = 71^{\circ}\), \(\beta = 11^{\circ}\).

Step 4: Put them together
\[\text{L.H.S.} = \dfrac{1}{2}\left[\sin 30^{\circ} + \sin 8^{\circ}\right.\]
\[\left.\quad - \cos 82^{\circ} + \cos 60^{\circ}\right]\]
Why: we simply replace both products by their sums.

Step 5: Use complementary angles and standard values
\[\cos 82^{\circ} = \cos(90^{\circ} - 8^{\circ}) = \sin 8^{\circ}\]
\[\text{L.H.S.}\]
\[= \dfrac{1}{2}\left[\dfrac{1}{2} + \sin 8^{\circ} - \sin 8^{\circ} + \dfrac{1}{2}\right]\]
\[= \dfrac{1}{2}\left[\dfrac{1}{2} + \dfrac{1}{2}\right] = \dfrac{1}{2} = \text{R.H.S.}\]
Why: \(\cos(90^{\circ} - \theta) = \sin\theta\), so \(\cos 82^{\circ}\) and \(\sin 8^{\circ}\) cancel; \(\sin 30^{\circ} = \cos 60^{\circ} = \frac{1}{2}\).

Check: with approximate values
\[\sin 19^{\circ}\cos 11^{\circ} \approx 0.3256 \times 0.9816 \approx 0.3196\]
\[\sin 71^{\circ}\sin 11^{\circ} \approx 0.9455 \times 0.1908 \approx 0.1804\]
\[0.3196 + 0.1804 = 0.5000\]

blocks.title: Example 16
steps:
Given: \(\sin 5x + \sin 7x\).
To find: the same expression as a product.
Method: a sum of two sines, so use \(\sin P + \sin Q = 2\sin\frac{P + Q}{2}\cos\frac{P - Q}{2}\).

Step 1: Half sum and half difference
\[P = 5x, \quad Q = 7x\]
\[\dfrac{P + Q}{2} = \dfrac{12x}{2} = 6x\]
\[\dfrac{P - Q}{2} = \dfrac{-2x}{2} = -x\]
Why: these are the two angles that appear in the product.

Step 2: Apply the formula
\[\sin 5x + \sin 7x\]
\[= 2\sin\dfrac{5x + 7x}{2}\cos\dfrac{5x - 7x}{2}\]
\[= 2\sin 6x\cos(-x)\]
Why: put the half sum in the sine and the half difference in the cosine.

Step 3: Remove the negative angle
\[= 2\sin 6x\cos x \quad (\because \cos(-\theta) = \cos\theta)\]
Why: cosine is an even function, \(\cos(-x) = \cos x\). (Taking \(P = 7x\), \(Q = 5x\) gives \(\cos x\) directly.)

Check: take \(x = 15^{\circ}\).
\[\sin 75^{\circ} + \sin 105^{\circ} = 2\sin 75^{\circ}\]
\[2\sin 90^{\circ}\cos 15^{\circ} = 2\cos 15^{\circ} = 2\sin 75^{\circ}\]
since \(\cos 15^{\circ} = \sin 75^{\circ}\) and \(\sin 105^{\circ} = \sin 75^{\circ}\). Both sides agree.

blocks.title: Example 17
steps:
Given: \(\cos\theta + \cos 3\theta + \cos 5\theta + \cos 7\theta\).
To find: the same expression as a product.
Method: the formula \(\cos P + \cos Q\) handles two terms at a time, so group the four terms in two pairs, change each pair into a product, take out the common factor, and use the formula once more.

Step 1: Group in pairs
\[\cos\theta + \cos 3\theta + \cos 5\theta + \cos 7\theta\]
\[= (\cos 3\theta + \cos\theta) + (\cos 7\theta + \cos 5\theta)\]
Why: in each pair the half difference is \(\theta\), so both pairs will give a common factor \(\cos\theta\). Writing the bigger angle first keeps the angles positive.

Step 2: First pair
\[\cos 3\theta + \cos\theta\]
\[= 2\cos\dfrac{3\theta + \theta}{2}\cos\dfrac{3\theta - \theta}{2}\]
\[= 2\cos 2\theta\cos\theta\]
Why: \(\cos P + \cos Q = 2\cos\frac{P + Q}{2}\cos\frac{P - Q}{2}\) with \(P = 3\theta\), \(Q = \theta\).

Step 3: Second pair
\[\cos 7\theta + \cos 5\theta\]
\[= 2\cos\dfrac{7\theta + 5\theta}{2}\cos\dfrac{7\theta - 5\theta}{2}\]
\[= 2\cos 6\theta\cos\theta\]
Why: same formula with \(P = 7\theta\), \(Q = 5\theta\). (The book prints the first fraction as \(\frac{7\theta + \theta}{2}\); it must be \(\frac{7\theta + 5\theta}{2} = 6\theta\), see the Book correction.)

Step 4: Take out the common factor
\[= 2\cos 2\theta\cos\theta + 2\cos 6\theta\cos\theta\]
\[= 2\cos\theta(\cos 6\theta + \cos 2\theta)\]
Why: \(2\cos\theta\) is common to both terms.

Step 5: Use the formula again
\[\cos 6\theta + \cos 2\theta\]
\[= 2\cos\dfrac{6\theta + 2\theta}{2}\cos\dfrac{6\theta - 2\theta}{2}\]
\[= 2\cos 4\theta\cos 2\theta\]
Why: the bracket is again a sum of two cosines.

Step 6: Write the product
\[= 2\cos\theta(2\cos 4\theta\cos 2\theta)\]
\[= 4\cos\theta\cos 2\theta\cos 4\theta\]
Why: \(2 \times 2 = 4\); the order of the factors does not matter.

Check:
\[\theta = 0^{\circ}: \ 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 = 4 = 4(1)(1)(1)\]
\[\theta = 30^{\circ}: \ \tfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} + 0 - \tfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} - \tfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} = -\tfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\]
\[4\cdot\tfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\cdot\tfrac{1}{2}\cdot\left(-\tfrac{1}{2}\right) = -\tfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\]

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: In Example 17 the book prints the second pair as \(2\cos\frac{7\theta + \theta}{2}\cos\frac{7\theta - 5\theta}{2}\). The pair is \(\cos 7\theta + \cos 5\theta\), so it must be \(2\cos\frac{7\theta + 5\theta}{2}\cos\frac{7\theta - 5\theta}{2} = 2\cos 6\theta\cos\theta\). The book's next line (\(2\cos 6\theta\cos\theta\)) is correct.

blocks.title: Example 18
steps:
Given: \(\cos 20^{\circ}\cos 40^{\circ}\cos 80^{\circ}\).
To prove: the product equals \(\frac{1}{8}\).
Method: there are three cosines. Use \(2\cos\alpha\cos\beta = \cos(\alpha + \beta) + \cos(\alpha - \beta)\) on two of them at a time; to have the factors 2 we multiply and divide by 4. Then \(\cos(180^{\circ} - \theta) = -\cos\theta\) cancels the unknown values.

Step 1: Create two factors of 2
\[\text{L.H.S.} = \cos 20^{\circ}\cos 40^{\circ}\cos 80^{\circ}\]
\[= \dfrac{1}{4}(4\cos 20^{\circ}\cos 40^{\circ}\cos 80^{\circ})\]
\[= \dfrac{1}{4}\left[(2\cos 40^{\circ}\cos 20^{\circ})\cdot 2\cos 80^{\circ}\right]\]
Why: \(\frac{1}{4} \times 4 = 1\), so the value is unchanged; \(4 = 2 \times 2\) gives one 2 for each product formula.

Step 2: First product
\[2\cos 40^{\circ}\cos 20^{\circ} = \cos 60^{\circ} + \cos 20^{\circ}\]
\[= \dfrac{1}{2} + \cos 20^{\circ}\]
Why: \(\alpha = 40^{\circ}\), \(\beta = 20^{\circ}\), so \(\alpha + \beta = 60^{\circ}\), \(\alpha - \beta = 20^{\circ}\), and \(\cos 60^{\circ} = \frac{1}{2}\).

Step 3: Multiply out
\[= \dfrac{1}{4}\left[\left(\dfrac{1}{2} + \cos 20^{\circ}\right)2\cos 80^{\circ}\right]\]
\[= \dfrac{1}{4}(\cos 80^{\circ} + 2\cos 80^{\circ}\cos 20^{\circ})\]
Why: \(\frac{1}{2} \times 2\cos 80^{\circ} = \cos 80^{\circ}\).

Step 4: Second product
\[2\cos 80^{\circ}\cos 20^{\circ} = \cos 100^{\circ} + \cos 60^{\circ}\]
\[= \dfrac{1}{4}(\cos 80^{\circ} + \cos 100^{\circ} + \cos 60^{\circ})\]
Why: \(\alpha = 80^{\circ}\), \(\beta = 20^{\circ}\): \(80^{\circ} + 20^{\circ} = 100^{\circ}\), \(80^{\circ} - 20^{\circ} = 60^{\circ}\).

Step 5: Use the allied angle
\[\cos 100^{\circ} = \cos(180^{\circ} - 80^{\circ}) = -\cos 80^{\circ}\]
\[= \dfrac{1}{4}\left[\cos 80^{\circ} - \cos 80^{\circ} + \dfrac{1}{2}\right]\]
\[= \dfrac{1}{4}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right) = \dfrac{1}{8} = \text{R.H.S.}\]
Why: \(\cos(180^{\circ} - \theta) = -\cos\theta\) (10.2), so \(\cos 80^{\circ}\) cancels.

Check: with approximate values
\[0.9397 \times 0.7660 \times 0.1736 \approx 0.1250 = \dfrac{1}{8}\]

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. Product to sum: \(2\sin\alpha\cos\beta = \sin(\alpha + \beta) + \sin(\alpha - \beta)\), \(2\cos\alpha\sin\beta = \sin(\alpha + \beta) - \sin(\alpha - \beta)\), \(2\cos\alpha\cos\beta = \cos(\alpha + \beta) + \cos(\alpha - \beta)\), \(-2\sin\alpha\sin\beta = \cos(\alpha + \beta) - \cos(\alpha - \beta)\).
2. Sum to product: half sum and half difference, \(\frac{P + Q}{2}\) and \(\frac{P - Q}{2}\).
3. Only \(\sin\sin\) and \(\cos P - \cos Q\) carry a minus sign.
4. Missing factor 2? Multiply and divide by 2 (or by 4 for three factors).
5. Use \(\cos(-\theta) = \cos\theta\), \(\sin(-\theta) = -\sin\theta\), \(\cos(90^{\circ} - \theta) = \sin\theta\), \(\cos(180^{\circ} - \theta) = -\cos\theta\) to finish.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
1. Forgetting the minus sign: \(\cos P - \cos Q = -2\sin\frac{P + Q}{2}\sin\frac{P - Q}{2}\), and \(2\sin\alpha\sin\beta = \cos(\alpha - \beta) - \cos(\alpha + \beta)\).
2. Using a product formula without the factor 2: \(\sin\alpha\cos\beta = \frac{1}{2}[\sin(\alpha + \beta) + \sin(\alpha - \beta)]\).
3. Taking the full sum instead of the half sum: \(\sin 5x + \sin 7x \ne 2\sin 12x\cos 2x\).
4. Mixing the first two box lines: \(\sin\cos\) gives a plus, \(\cos\sin\) gives a minus.
